Data Science with Generative AI: Applications to Business
Robust Data Modeling with Ensembling and Tuning Techniques
Visa Approval Facilitation

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

Business communities in the United States are facing high demand for human resources, but one of the constant challenges is identifying and attracting the right talent, which is perhaps the most important element in remaining competitive. Companies in the United States look for hard-working, talented, and qualified individuals both locally as well as abroad.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of the US permits foreign workers to come to the United States to work on either a temporary or permanent basis. The act also protects US workers against adverse impacts on their wages or working conditions by ensuring US employers' compliance with statutory requirements when they hire foreign workers to fill workforce shortages. The immigration programs are administered by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).

OFLC processes job certification applications for employers seeking to bring foreign workers into the United States and grants certifications in those cases where employers can demonstrate that there are not sufficient US workers available to perform the work at wages that meet or exceed the wage paid for the occupation in the area of intended employment.

Objective¶

In FY 2016, the OFLC processed 775,979 employer applications for 1,699,957 positions for temporary and permanent labor certifications. This was a nine percent increase in the overall number of processed applications from the previous year. The process of reviewing every case is becoming a tedious task as the number of applicants is increasing every year.

The increasing number of applicants every year calls for a Machine Learning based solution that can help in shortlisting the candidates having higher chances of VISA approval. OFLC has hired the firm EasyVisa for data-driven solutions. You as a data scientist at EasyVisa have to analyze the data provided and, with the help of a classification model:

  • Facilitate the process of visa approvals.
  • Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of employee and the employer. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • case_id: ID of each visa application
  • continent: Information of continent the employee
  • education_of_employee: Information of education of the employee
  • has_job_experience: Does the employee has any job experience? Y= Yes; N = No
  • requires_job_training: Does the employee require any job training? Y = Yes; N = No
  • no_of_employees: Number of employees in the employer's company
  • yr_of_estab: Year in which the employer's company was established
  • region_of_employment: Information of foreign worker's intended region of employment in the US.
  • prevailing_wage: Average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment. The purpose of the prevailing wage is to ensure that the foreign worker is not underpaid compared to other workers offering the same or similar service in the same area of employment.
  • unit_of_wage: Unit of prevailing wage. Values include Hourly, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly.
  • full_time_position: Is the position of work full-time? Y = Full Time Position; N = Part Time Position
  • case_status: Flag indicating if the Visa was certified or denied

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Below is a brief EDA of the most salient features. A full EDA can be found in the Appendix Section.

  • EDA is an important part of any project involving data.
  • It is important to investigate and understand the data better before building a model with it.
  • A few questions have been mentioned below which will help you approach the analysis in the right manner and generate insights from the data.
  • A thorough analysis of the data, in addition to the questions mentioned below, should be done.

Leading Questions

What is the distribution of visa case statuses (certified vs. denied)?

  1. What is the distribution of visa case statuses (certified vs. denied)?
  2. How does the education level of employees impact visa approval rates?
  3. Is there a significant difference in visa approval rates between employees with and without prior job experience?
  4. How does the prevailing wage affect visa approval? Do higher wages lead to higher chances of approval?
  5. Do certain regions in the US have higher visa approval rates compared to others?
  6. How does the number of employees in a company influence visa approval? Do larger companies have a higher approval rate?
  7. Are visa approval rates different across various continents of employees? Which continent has the highest and lowest approval rates?

#custom definitions from the course to visualize data
def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(15, 10), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (15,10))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a triangle will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram


  # function to create labeled barplots
def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 2, 6))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 2, 6))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        hue=feature, # Added to address FutureWarning
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
        legend=False # Added to address FutureWarning
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 5, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left", frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

There are 33 observations out of the 25,480 observations. This accounts for 0.1295% of the data. There are three possible explanations for this value:

  1. The negative was a dash indicator rather than a negative sign, in which case dropping the negative value would be best.
  2. The negative sign on a 10-key pad is nearest to the 9. It is possible that each of these values should be in the 900s. However, this is less likely since companies start reporting rounded figures at roughly the 250 employee count.
  3. These are pure data entry meaning they should be deleted.

While I am tempted to use the absolute value for these, the distribution of companies across regional areas, education levels, continents, etc suggest that we will not lose too much data. These values will be dropped.

Feature Engineering¶

Feature Engineering on prevailing_wage¶

The goal of this code to to adjust prevailing wage into all the same unit of measure, whether yearly or annual. Since there is a relatively high number of part time positions, it only makes sense to adjust the wage to an annual rate.

In [38]:
# 1) copy the dataframe to a new one called test_data
test_data = viz_data.copy()
In [39]:
# 2) copy the prevailing_wage column to a new column titled adj_wage
test_data['adj_wage'] = test_data['prevailing_wage'].copy()

# Clean the 'unit_of_wage' column first for consistent comparisons
test_data['unit_of_wage'] = test_data['unit_of_wage'].str.strip().str.lower()

# 3) if the unit_of_wage = "hour" and if full_time_position = "Y", then multiply the corresponding value of adj_wage
# using this formula: adj_wage = adj_wage * 40 * 52 and overwrite the original value of adj_wage
test_data.loc[
    (test_data['unit_of_wage'] == 'hour') & (test_data['full_time_position'] == 'Y'),
    'adj_wage'
] = test_data['adj_wage'] * 40 * 52
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage']== 'hour') & (test_data["full_time_position"] == 'Y'), 'unit_of_wage'] = "year"

# 4) if the unit_of_wage = "week" then multiply using the formula: adj_wage = adj_wage * 52
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage'] == 'week'),'adj_wage'] = test_data['adj_wage'] * 52
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage']== 'week'), 'unit_of_wage'] = "year"

# 5) if the unit_of_wage = "month"  then use the formula adj_wage = adj_wage * 12
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage'] == 'month'),'adj_wage'] = test_data['adj_wage'] * 12
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage']== 'month'), 'unit_of_wage'] = "year"

# Filter test_data to remove outliers based on the same logic used for viz_data_trimmed earlier,
# or re-calculate for test_data if 'adj_wage' has different outlier characteristics.
# For now, let's assume we want to show the KDE for the original data to match the first boxplot, or filter the outliers here.
# A more robust approach might re-calculate IQR for 'adj_wage' in test_data.

# Calculate IQR for 'adj_wage' in test_data for accurate outlier removal for the KDE plot
Q1_adj = test_data['adj_wage'].quantile(0.25)
Q3_adj = test_data['adj_wage'].quantile(0.75)
IQR_adj = Q3_adj - Q1_adj
lower_bound_adj = Q1_adj - 1.5 * IQR_adj
upper_bound_adj = Q3_adj + 1.5 * IQR_adj

test_data_trimmed_adj = test_data[(test_data['adj_wage'] >= lower_bound_adj) & (test_data['adj_wage'] <= upper_bound_adj)]

sns.kdeplot(data=test_data_trimmed_adj, x="adj_wage", hue="full_time_position", fill=True, ax=axes[1, 1])
axes[1, 1].set_title("Density Plot of Adjusted Wage (without outliers)")
axes[1, 1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.FormatStrFormatter('%.0e'))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

There is still significant overlap in both the part time and full time job categories, suggest that the feature engineering did not introduce any unintentional skew into the data.

Having worked overseas myself, I know that there is often a minimal salary threshhold for obtaining a post. As a result, many of the lower values in the adjusted wage category seem suspect (such as the $99.999 annual wage). The confusion may have resulted from the fact that the USA uses a comma (,) to separate groups of thousands while other countries use periods (.) for this same principle. However, there are a very high number of adj_wage values that are less than $30,000. without more information, any more adjustment to this column would be arbitrary. There is too much data to drop. As a result, these values, though odd, will remain. However, in order to reduce the granularity of the data, I will group the adjusted wage into five categorical variables using quantiles.

Feature engineering - year established¶

The year established (1800 to 2016) might not be the best way to view these categories since older companies would have a lower value. As a result, I will create a new category called yrs_in_bus by subtracting the founding year from 2016 (the most recent year in the dataset).

There is virtually no correlation between any of the numeric values. There is a lack of correlation between adjusted wage and prevailing wage; however, due to the different units reported for the wage, this is not wholely unexpected. As a result of this feature engineering, prevailing_wage and unit_of_wage can be dropped. Not surprising, there is a perfectly negative correlation between yrs_in_bus and yr_of_estab, so one of these will be dropped.

Outlier Treatment¶

In [50]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# use a loop to display boxplots for all the numeric variable in the test_data data frame
numeric_columns = test_data.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 12))

plot_idx = 1 # Initialize a counter for subplot positions

for variable in numeric_columns:
    # Plot with outliers
    ax1 = plt.subplot(5, 2, plot_idx) # Changed from 4 to 5 rows
    ax1.boxplot(test_data[variable], whis=1.5)
    ax1.set_title(f'{variable} (with outliers)')
    plot_idx += 1

    # Plot without outliers
    ax2 = plt.subplot(5, 2, plot_idx) # Changed from 4 to 5 rows
    ax2.boxplot(test_data[variable], whis=1.5, showfliers=False, showmeans=True)
    ax2.set_title(f'{variable} (without outliers)')
    plot_idx += 1

plt.tight_layout() # Call tight_layout once after all subplots are created
plt.show()

All outliers are within reasonable expectations for wage, company size, and year founded. As a result, none of them will be treated.

Observations on case_status, full_time_position, and wage_category¶

In [56]:
# Ensure 'wage_category', 'full_time_position', and 'case_status' are categorical
# 'wage_category' is already ordered from previous steps.
if not isinstance(data1['full_time_position'].dtype, pd.CategoricalDtype):
    data1['full_time_position'] = data1['full_time_position'].astype('category')
if not isinstance(data1['case_status'].dtype, pd.CategoricalDtype):
    data1['case_status'] = data1['case_status'].astype('category')

# Create a mapping for full_time_position labels (Y/N to Full Time/Part Time)
position_map = {
    'Y': 'Full Time',
    'N': 'Part Time'
}
data1['full_time_position_label'] = data1['full_time_position'].map(position_map).astype('category')

# Group data to get counts for each combination of wage_category, full_time_position_label, and case_status
plot_df_counts = data1.groupby(['wage_category', 'full_time_position_label', 'case_status'], observed=True).size().unstack(level='case_status').fillna(0)

# Calculate proportions within each full_time_position_label for each wage_category
# This makes each 'Full Time' bar sum to 1 and each 'Part Time' bar sum to 1
# Corrected calculation for plot_df to properly normalize proportions
plot_df = plot_df_counts.div(plot_df_counts.sum(axis=1), axis=0)

# Define a darker color scheme for better readability as requested previously
colors = {
    ('Full Time', 'Certified'): 'darkslategray',
    ('Full Time', 'Denied'): 'firebrick',
    ('Part Time', 'Certified'): 'lightslategray',
    ('Part Time', 'Denied'): 'lightcoral'
}

# Get ordered wage categories from the DataFrame's categorical dtype
wage_categories_ordered = data1['wage_category'].cat.categories.tolist()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(15, 8))

# Position of each group of bars on the x-axis
ind = np.arange(len(wage_categories_ordered))
width = 0.35 # Width of the bars for Full Time/Part Time

for i, category in enumerate(wage_categories_ordered):
    # Get data for 'Full Time' and 'Part Time' for the current wage category
    # Use .get() with a default empty Series to handle cases where a combination might not exist after proportion calculation
    full_time_data = plot_df.loc[(category, 'Full Time')] if (category, 'Full Time') in plot_df.index else pd.Series({'Certified': 0, 'Denied': 0})
    part_time_data = plot_df.loc[(category, 'Part Time')] if (category, 'Part Time') in plot_df.index else pd.Series({'Certified': 0, 'Denied': 0})

    # Plot 'Full Time' bars (Certified and Denied stacked)
    bottom_full_time = 0
    if 'Certified' in full_time_data.index and full_time_data['Certified'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] - width/2, full_time_data['Certified'], width,
               bottom=bottom_full_time,
               label='Full Time - Certified' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Full Time', 'Certified')], edgecolor='white')
        bottom_full_time += full_time_data['Certified']
    if 'Denied' in full_time_data.index and full_time_data['Denied'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] - width/2, full_time_data['Denied'], width,
               bottom=bottom_full_time,
               label='Full Time - Denied' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Full Time', 'Denied')], edgecolor='white')

    # Plot 'Part Time' bars (Certified and Denied stacked)
    bottom_part_time = 0
    if 'Certified' in part_time_data.index and part_time_data['Certified'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] + width/2, part_time_data['Certified'], width,
               bottom=bottom_part_time,
               label='Part Time - Certified' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Part Time', 'Certified')], edgecolor='white')
        bottom_part_time += part_time_data['Certified']
    if 'Denied' in part_time_data.index and part_time_data['Denied'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] + width/2, part_time_data['Denied'], width,
               bottom=bottom_part_time,
               label='Part Time - Denied' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Part Time', 'Denied')], edgecolor='white')

ax.set_ylabel('Proportion', fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlabel('Wage Category', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Visa Case Status Proportion by Full-Time Position and Wage Category', fontsize=16)
ax.set_xticks(ind)
ax.set_xticklabels(wage_categories_ordered, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=10)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1) # Set y-axis limit for proportions from 0 to 1

# Create a custom legend using Patch objects
legend_patches = [
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Full Time', 'Certified')], label='Full Time - Certified'),
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Full Time', 'Denied')], label='Full Time - Denied'),
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Part Time', 'Certified')], label='Part Time - Certified'),
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Part Time', 'Denied')], label='Part Time - Denied')
]
ax.legend(handles=legend_patches, title="Case Status & Position Type", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left', fontsize=10, title_fontsize=12)

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 0.85, 1]) # Adjust rect to make space for the legend
plt.show()

Several visualizations were attempted here (see Appendix) in order to better understand the relationship between the response variable (case_study), a full time position, and the engineered wage categories. I had assumed that these two independent categories would have an impact on the result of the case. However, there is significant overlap among the categories. The only true surprise is that full time workers earning a wage in the top 20% of wages had a much higher proportion of denied applications than did the other groups. The other is a more general trend: it appears that the higher the wage, the more likely a visa will be declined.

sns.boxplot(data=data1, x='case_status', y='adj_wage', hue='full_time_position', showmeans=True, showfliers=False, ax=axes[1])

axes[1].set_xlabel('Case Status') # Keep x-label for the bottom plot
axes[1].set_ylabel('Adjusted Wage (Annual)') # Keep y-label as it's a new row
axes[1].ticklabel_format(style='plain', axis='y') # Disable scientific notation for y-axis

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

For approved visas, part time position adjusted wages had a higher median and greater range than did wages for full time positions. However, this may be due to the presence of some signficant outliers. The medians for both full time and part time jobs that were denied visas are roughly equivalent.

Model Building¶

Model evaluation criterion¶

The model can make wrong predictions as:

  1. Model predicts that the visa application will get certified but in reality, the visa application should get denied.
  2. Model predicts that the visa application will not get certified but in reality, the visa application should get certified.

Which case is more important?

In this context, both of the cases are important:

  1. If a visa is certified when it had to be denied a wrong employee will get the job position while US citizens will miss the opportunity to work on that position.

  2. However, if a visa is denied when it had to be certified the U.S. will lose a suitable human resource that can contribute to the economy.

How to reduce the losses?

I will be using F1 Score: the greater the F1 score higher are the chances of minimizing both False Negatives and False Positives. We will use balanced class weights so that model focuses equally on both classes.

In [60]:
#custom functions for model comparison taken from the course

def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

Model Performance Improvement¶

Note¶

  1. Sample parameter grids have been provided to do necessary hyperparameter tuning. These sample grids are expected to provide a balance between model performance improvement and execution time. One can extend/reduce the parameter grid based on execution time and system configuration.
  • Please note that if the parameter grid is extended to improve the model performance further, the execution time will increase
  1. The models chosen in this notebook are based on test runs. One can update the best models as obtained upon code execution and tune them for best performance.
  • For Gradient Boosting:
param_grid = {
    "init": [AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=1),DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1)],
    "n_estimators": np.arange(50,110,25),
    "learning_rate": [0.01,0.1,0.05],
    "subsample":[0.7,0.9],
    "max_features":[0.5,0.7,1],
}
  • For Adaboost:
param_grid = {
    "n_estimators": np.arange(50,110,25),
    "learning_rate": [0.01,0.1,0.05],
    "base_estimator": [
        DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=1),
        DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=1),
    ],
}
  • For Bagging Classifier:
param_grid = {
    'max_samples': [0.8,0.9,1],
    'max_features': [0.7,0.8,0.9],
    'n_estimators' : [30,50,70],
}
  • For Random Forest:
param_grid = {
    "n_estimators": [50,110,25],
    "min_samples_leaf": np.arange(1, 4),
    "max_features": [np.arange(0.3, 0.6, 0.1),'sqrt'],
    "max_samples": np.arange(0.4, 0.7, 0.1)
}
  • For Decision Trees:
param_grid = {
    'max_depth': np.arange(2,6),
    'min_samples_leaf': [1, 4, 7],
    'max_leaf_nodes' : [10, 15],
    'min_impurity_decrease': [0.0001,0.001]
}
  • For XGBoost:
param_grid={'n_estimators':np.arange(50,110,25),
            'scale_pos_weight':[1,2,5],
            'learning_rate':[0.01,0.1,0.05],
            'gamma':[1,3],
            'subsample':[0.7,0.9]
}

In the original test set, only AdaBoost and Gradient Boost seemed to strike a good balance in the F1 score between training and validation sets. However, since hypertuning has to potential to improve a model, and for the sake of completeness, I will hypertune all five of the models. Furthermore, since there was a small gain to be had with oversampling versus the original data, I will be using the oversampled data for these tuned models.

After doing some internet research, I learned that there is the possiblity of data leakage when running SMOTE before GridSearchCV. The problem is that some of the same data points can appear in the cross validation folds. This means that the final fitted model can still appear to be much stronger than the actual model when applying the tuned model back to X_train and y_train. Thus, I added the pipeline function which ensures that smote occurs after the fold step. I will be using this method for all five of the tuned models.

Hyperparameter Tuning - Bagging¶

In [66]:
%%time
# Choose the type of classifer
bag_tuned = BaggingClassifier(random_state=1)

# 1. Define a pipeline that chains SMOTE and Random Forest together
bag_pipeline = ImbPipeline([
    ('smote', SMOTE(random_state=1)),
    ('bag', BaggingClassifier(estimator=DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1), random_state=1)) # Explicitly define the base estimator
])

# 2. Define parameters

parameters = {
    'bag__max_samples': [0.8,0.9,1],
    'bag__max_features': [0.7,0.8,0.9],
    'bag__n_estimators' : [30,50,70],
    'bag__estimator__max_depth': [5, 10, 15], # Add tuning for base estimator's max_depth
    'bag__estimator__min_samples_leaf': [1, 2, 4] # Add tuning for base estimator's min_samples_leaf
}
# Type of scoring used to compare parameter combinations
acc_scorer = metrics.make_scorer(metrics.f1_score)

# 3. Run the grid search
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(bag_pipeline, parameters, scoring=acc_scorer, cv=5, n_jobs=-1)
grid_obj.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 4. Extract the ultimate tuned model
# This automatically includes the SMOTE step for final training
bag_best_model = grid_obj.best_estimator_

Feature Importances of the Final Model¶

In [102]:
#graph important features of the final model
feature_names = X_train.columns
importances =  final_model.feature_importances_
indices = np.argsort(importances)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 12))
plt.title("Feature Importances")
plt.barh(range(len(indices)), importances[indices], color="violet", align="center")
plt.yticks(range(len(indices)), [feature_names[i] for i in indices])
plt.xlabel("Relative Importance")
plt.show()

From the chart above, the engineered category of adjusted wage (adj_wage) was the most significant feature in predicting the result of the model. The second most important feature was high school level of education followed by the number of employees.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Conclusions¶

  1. This predictive model can identify the key features that influence a decision on a visa application: whether certified or denied.
  2. Key features that influence visa decisions are:
    • adjusted wage: wages that are higher than average are more likely to be denied
    • high school level of education: having only a high school level of education is likely to lead to a denial
    • number of company employees: larger companies are more likely to see a visa approval
    • years in business: older companies are more likely to see approvals
    • has prior job experience: prior job experience is more likely to lead to an approval
    • has an advanced degree (either Master's or Doctorate: advanced degrees are more likely to lead to approvals
    • being of European or North American origin increases the likelihood of approval
    • being employed in the West and Midwest improves the chances of getting approved
  3. All other features have at least some bearing on the prediction, but one that is less than 2% of the decision.

Business Recommendations¶

  1. The profile of a highly qualified candidate who is likely to get approved for a visa is someone who holds an advanced degree and is offered a wage that is not exorbiatantly higher than the average of this data set. While different jobs obviously qualify for different levels of compensation, a company could stratigically lower the initial offer to the qualified candidate and make up the difference in bonuses and raises after the visa approval has been finalized and the work commenced.
  2. The company should recommend against pursuing candidates with only a high school degree. These candidates are more likely to be denied than others.
  3. The company should prioritze and fast track those applicants who have prior work experience.
  4. Companies should prioritize hiring local (US Citizens) for jobs not located in the West or Midwest, while companies in these locations are more likely to have their candidates approved.

Two features beyond a company's direct control which strongly affect visa decisions are the number of employees and the year the company was established. In order to mitigate these influeces, smaller companies with shorter established tenures should make meeting the four guidelines above a much higher priority.

There is significant overlap in the wages between full time and part time positions. Both are right skewed and the ranges are nearly identical. Oddly, the lowest wage (though not technically classifed as an outlier) of $2.1367 is from the full tiem group. This number is a bit odd since it is clearly a wage that has been adjust to show hourly (since the USA only uses cents out to the hundredths decimal place). This suggests that prevailing_wage will end up not being a very useful analysis category without feature engineering.

Feature Engineering on prevailing_wage¶

The goal of this code to to adjust prevailing wage into all the same unit of measure, whether yearly or annual. Since there is a relatively high number of part time positions, it only makes sense to adjust the wage to an annual rate.

In [139]:
# 1) copy the dataframe to a new one called test_data
test_data = viz_data.copy()
In [140]:
# 2) copy the prevailing_wage column to a new column titled adj_wage
test_data['adj_wage'] = test_data['prevailing_wage'].copy()

# Clean the 'unit_of_wage' column first for consistent comparisons
test_data['unit_of_wage'] = test_data['unit_of_wage'].str.strip().str.lower()

# 3) if the unit_of_wage = "hour" and if full_time_position = "Y", then multiply the corresponding value of adj_wage
# using this formula: adj_wage = adj_wage * 40 * 52 and overwrite the original value of adj_wage
test_data.loc[
    (test_data['unit_of_wage'] == 'hour') & (test_data['full_time_position'] == 'Y'),
    'adj_wage'
] = test_data['adj_wage'] * 40 * 52
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage']== 'hour') & (test_data["full_time_position"] == 'Y'), 'unit_of_wage'] = "year"

# 4) if the unit_of_wage = "week" then multiply using the formula: adj_wage = adj_wage * 52
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage'] == 'week'),'adj_wage'] = test_data['adj_wage'] * 52
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage']== 'week'), 'unit_of_wage'] = "year"

# 5) if the unit_of_wage = "month"  then use the formula adj_wage = adj_wage * 12
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage'] == 'month'),'adj_wage'] = test_data['adj_wage'] * 12
test_data.loc[(test_data['unit_of_wage']== 'month'), 'unit_of_wage'] = "year"

# Fourth subplot (bottom-right): KDE plot for data without outliers
# Filter test_data to remove outliers based on the same logic used for viz_data_trimmed earlier,
# or re-calculate for test_data if 'adj_wage' has different outlier characteristics.
# For now, let's assume we want to show the KDE for the original data to match the first boxplot, or filter the outliers here.
# A more robust approach might re-calculate IQR for 'adj_wage' in test_data.

# Calculate IQR for 'adj_wage' in test_data for accurate outlier removal for the KDE plot
Q1_adj = test_data['adj_wage'].quantile(0.25)
Q3_adj = test_data['adj_wage'].quantile(0.75)
IQR_adj = Q3_adj - Q1_adj
lower_bound_adj = Q1_adj - 1.5 * IQR_adj
upper_bound_adj = Q3_adj + 1.5 * IQR_adj

test_data_trimmed_adj = test_data[(test_data['adj_wage'] >= lower_bound_adj) & (test_data['adj_wage'] <= upper_bound_adj)]

sns.kdeplot(data=test_data_trimmed_adj, x="adj_wage", hue="full_time_position", fill=True, ax=axes[1, 1])
axes[1, 1].set_title("Density Plot of Adjusted Wage (without outliers)")
axes[1, 1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.FormatStrFormatter('%.0e'))

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

There is still significant overlap in both the part time and full time job categories, suggest that the feature engineering did not introduce any unintentional skew into the data.

Having worked overseas myself, I know that there is often a minimal salary threshhold for obtaining a post. As a result, many of the lower values in the adjusted wage category seem suspect (such as the $99.999 annual wage). The confusion may have resulted from the fact that the USA uses a comma (,) to separate groups of thousands while other countries use periods (.) for this same principle. However, there are a very high number of adj_wage values that are less than $30,000. without more information, any more adjustment to this column would be arbitrary. There is too much data to drop. As a result, these values, though odd, will remain.

from statsmodels.graphics.mosaicplot import mosaic
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

# Increase width of the graph
plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (15, 8)

# Define custom colors
colors_map = {
    'Certified': 'darkgray',    # Dark gray for Certified
    'Denied': 'lightcoral'    # Pale red/orange for Denied
}

# Function to apply custom colors to the mosaic plot tiles
def properties_func_updated(key):
    status = key[-1] # Get the 'case_status' value from the key
    return {'facecolor': colors_map.get(status, 'lightgray'), 'edgecolor': 'white'}

# Create the mosaic plot
# The mosaic function returns the Figure (fig) and a dictionary of rectangles (rect_dict).
# The Axes object needs to be explicitly retrieved from the Figure.
fig, rect_dict = mosaic(test_data, ['full_time_position', 'wage_category', 'case_status'],
                     properties=properties_func_updated, # Apply custom coloring
                     title='Mosaic Plot of Case Status by Full-Time Position and Wage Category',
                     gap=0.01)

# Get the Axes object from the Figure
ax = fig.gca()

# Add a key (legend) to explain the color coding
legend_elements = [Patch(facecolor=colors_map[status], label=status)
                   for status in colors_map]

ax.legend(handles=legend_elements, title="Case Status", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left', borderaxespad=0.)

# Ensure the layout is tight to prevent labels/legend from being cut off
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 0.85, 1]) # Adjust rect to make space for the legend on the right

plt.show()

    'Y': 'Full Time',
    'N': 'Part Time'
}
test_data['full_time_position_label'] = test_data['full_time_position'].map(position_map).astype('category')

# Group data to get counts for each combination of wage_category, full_time_position_label, and case_status
plot_df_counts = test_data.groupby(['wage_category', 'full_time_position_label', 'case_status'], observed=True).size().unstack(level='case_status').fillna(0)

# Calculate proportions within each full_time_position_label for each wage_category
# This makes each 'Full Time' bar sum to 1 and each 'Part Time' bar sum to 1
# Corrected calculation for plot_df to properly normalize proportions
plot_df = plot_df_counts.div(plot_df_counts.sum(axis=1), axis=0)

# Define a darker color scheme for better readability as requested previously
colors = {
    ('Full Time', 'Certified'): 'darkslategray',
    ('Full Time', 'Denied'): 'firebrick',
    ('Part Time', 'Certified'): 'lightslategray',
    ('Part Time', 'Denied'): 'lightcoral'
}

# Get ordered wage categories from the DataFrame's categorical dtype
wage_categories_ordered = test_data['wage_category'].cat.categories.tolist()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(15, 8))

# Position of each group of bars on the x-axis
ind = np.arange(len(wage_categories_ordered))
width = 0.35 # Width of the bars for Full Time/Part Time

for i, category in enumerate(wage_categories_ordered):
    # Get data for 'Full Time' and 'Part Time' for the current wage category
    # Use .get() with a default empty Series to handle cases where a combination might not exist after proportion calculation
    full_time_data = plot_df.loc[(category, 'Full Time')] if (category, 'Full Time') in plot_df.index else pd.Series({'Certified': 0, 'Denied': 0})
    part_time_data = plot_df.loc[(category, 'Part Time')] if (category, 'Part Time') in plot_df.index else pd.Series({'Certified': 0, 'Denied': 0})

    # Plot 'Full Time' bars (Certified and Denied stacked)
    bottom_full_time = 0
    if 'Certified' in full_time_data.index and full_time_data['Certified'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] - width/2, full_time_data['Certified'], width,
               bottom=bottom_full_time,
               label='Full Time - Certified' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Full Time', 'Certified')], edgecolor='white')
        bottom_full_time += full_time_data['Certified']
    if 'Denied' in full_time_data.index and full_time_data['Denied'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] - width/2, full_time_data['Denied'], width,
               bottom=bottom_full_time,
               label='Full Time - Denied' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Full Time', 'Denied')], edgecolor='white')

    # Plot 'Part Time' bars (Certified and Denied stacked)
    bottom_part_time = 0
    if 'Certified' in part_time_data.index and part_time_data['Certified'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] + width/2, part_time_data['Certified'], width,
               bottom=bottom_part_time,
               label='Part Time - Certified' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Part Time', 'Certified')], edgecolor='white')
        bottom_part_time += part_time_data['Certified']
    if 'Denied' in part_time_data.index and part_time_data['Denied'] > 0:
        ax.bar(ind[i] + width/2, part_time_data['Denied'], width,
               bottom=bottom_part_time,
               label='Part Time - Denied' if i == 0 else "", # Label only once for legend
               color=colors[('Part Time', 'Denied')], edgecolor='white')

ax.set_ylabel('Proportion', fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlabel('Wage Category', fontsize=12)
ax.set_title('Visa Case Status Proportion by Full-Time Position and Wage Category', fontsize=16)
ax.set_xticks(ind)
ax.set_xticklabels(wage_categories_ordered, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=10)
ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1) # Set y-axis limit for proportions from 0 to 1

# Create a custom legend using Patch objects
legend_patches = [
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Full Time', 'Certified')], label='Full Time - Certified'),
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Full Time', 'Denied')], label='Full Time - Denied'),
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Part Time', 'Certified')], label='Part Time - Certified'),
    Patch(facecolor=colors[('Part Time', 'Denied')], label='Part Time - Denied')
]
ax.legend(handles=legend_patches, title="Case Status & Position Type", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left', fontsize=10, title_fontsize=12)

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 0.85, 1]) # Adjust rect to make space for the legend
plt.show()

Several visualizations were attempted here in order to better understand the relationship between the response variable (case_study), a full time position, and the engineered wage categories. I had assumed that these two independent categories would have an impact on the result of the case. However, there is significant overlap among the categories. The only true surprise is that full time workers earning a wage in the top 20% of wages had a much higher proportion of denied applications than did the other groups.

Observations on case_status, adj_wage, and full_time_position¶

# Create a figure with two subplots (2 rows, 1 column) for vertical arrangement
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 12), sharex=True) # sharex ensures x-axis scale is consistent, figsize adjusted for vertical

# Subplot 1 (top): Boxplot with outliers
sns.boxplot(data=test_data, x='case_status', y='adj_wage', hue='full_time_position', showmeans=True, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('Adjusted Wage Distribution by Case Status and Full-Time Position (with outliers)')
axes[0].set_xlabel('') # Remove x-label for top plot as it's shared and will be on the bottom plot
axes[0].set_ylabel('Adjusted Wage (Annual)')
axes[0].ticklabel_format(style='plain', axis='y') # Disable scientific notation for y-axis
axes[0].legend(title='Full-Time Position', bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')

# Subplot 2 (bottom): Boxplot without outliers
sns.boxplot(data=test_data, x='case_status', y='adj_wage', hue='full_time_position', showmeans=True, showfliers=False, ax=axes[1])

axes[1].set_xlabel('Case Status') # Keep x-label for the bottom plot
axes[1].set_ylabel('Adjusted Wage (Annual)') # Keep y-label as it's a new row

axes[1].legend(title='Full-Time Position', bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

For approved visas, part time position adjusted wages had a higher median and greater range than did wages for full time positions. However, this may be due to the presence of some signficant outliers. The medians for both full time and part time jobs that were denied visas are roughly equivalent.
